Vedic texts are ancient sacred literature in the public domain; summaries and translations are the author's own words. Prescribed sources referenced: Rig Veda (oldest Veda; 1,028 hymns); Sama, Yajur and Atharva Vedas; Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads; Mahabharata and Ramayana (epics); Iron artefacts and Painted Grey Ware (archaeology).

overview.intro: The Vedic Age (c. 1500-600 BCE) is named after the Vedas, our main literary source for the period. This chapter studies the four Vedas and the epics, the social organisation of the Early Vedic family and the position of the king, the Rig Vedic assemblies (Sabha, Samiti, Vidhatha), the changing position of women, the comparison between the Early and Later Vedic economy, and the four-fold class divisions, the four Ashramas and the education system.

blocks.text: The Aryans - tribes speaking Indo-Aryan dialects - migrated into India through the north-west after 1500 BCE, first settling in the Punjab and the Indus basin (the land of the seven rivers, Sapta Sindhava), and later spreading east to the Ganga-Yamuna doab. Our knowledge of them comes mainly from their own literature: the Vedas, composed and preserved orally with astonishing accuracy, supported by the epics and confirmed by iron artefacts and Painted Grey Ware pottery found by archaeologists. The period is divided into the Early (Rig) Vedic Age (c. 1500-1000 BCE, Rig Vedic) and the Later Vedic Age (c. 1000-600 BCE, the three other Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads).

Sources - the four Vedas and the epics. The Rig Veda is the oldest, a collection of 1,028 hymns praising the gods (Indra, Agni, Varuna, Soma); the Sama Veda sets selected Rig Vedic hymns to melody for singing; the Yajur Veda gives the formulae and rituals for sacrifices; the Atharva Veda contains charms, cures and folk beliefs reflecting daily life. Each Veda is linked to explanatory Brahmanas, forest treatises (Aranyakas) and philosophical Upanishads. The epics - the Mahabharata (traditionally by Vyasa) and the Ramayana (traditionally by Valmiki) - though finally compiled later, preserve memories of Later Vedic kingdoms, social norms and ideals of duty; they are crucial literary sources for the values of the age.

Early Vedic society - the family. Society was organised in patriarchal families: the father (grihapati) headed the household, and several families formed a village (grama), several villages a clan (vis), and clans the tribe (jana). The joint family was the norm; property was inherited by sons; the father's authority was firm but the family was bound by affection and shared sacrifice. Marriage was a samskara (sacrament), generally monogamous among the early people, and women took part in tribal assemblies and sacrifices; education was open to women in the early period (there are learned women hymn-composers such as Lopamudra and Ghosha).

The position of the king. The Early Vedic king (rajan) was a tribal war-leader chosen or accepted by the people, not an absolute monarch. He protected the tribe and cattle, led in battle, and performed sacrifices for the tribe's welfare. He was assisted by household officers (ratnins) and advised by the Sabha and Samiti; kingship depended on consent - the Aitareya Brahmana itself lists the people as one of the pillars of the state. The king received voluntary tribute (bali) rather than regular taxation, and lived simply, often in a thatched house.

Rig Vedic assemblies - Sabha, Samiti, Vidhatha. The Vidhatha was the oldest assembly, handling tribal business, distribution of booty and religious rites. The Samiti was the broad people's assembly that elected the king, discussed public affairs and could express disapproval of him. The Sabha was a smaller council of elders and nobles which advised the king and sat in judgment; later it came to mean the king's court. Together these bodies limited the king's power and gave Vedic polity its democratic spirit.

Position of women - Early vs Later Vedic. In Early Vedic society women enjoyed respect and freedom: they could be educated (women seers like Lopamudra, Apala, Ghosha composed hymns), attended assemblies, chose husbands in some cases (svayamvara in the epics), participated in sacrifices and were not veiled. Widow remarriage seems permissible. In the Later Vedic period the position declined sharply: education was largely denied to women, early marriage appeared, the doctrine that a woman depended on father, husband and son was preached, veiling and sati-like ideals spread among some classes, and women lost their place in public assemblies. The change followed settled agriculture, the hardening of the varna system and the growth of ritual religion.

Economy - Early vs Later Vedic. Early Vedic economy was pastoral and semi-nomadic: cattle were the chief wealth (the word for war, gavishthi, means 'search for cows'), land was tribal, agriculture existed (hymn to the plough) but was secondary, and there was barter (cows as units of value, nishka gold ornament as high-value exchange) with little craft specialisation. In the Later Vedic period, the iron ploughshare and irrigation transformed agriculture into the main occupation; villages were permanent; crafts (weaving, leather, metallurgy, pottery - Painted Grey Ware) and trade specialised; coins (nishka, satamana) and early traders' guild-like groups (shreshthi) appeared; land ownership became individual and land revenue (bali) was regularised. Society moved from pastoral tribe to agrarian kingdom.

The four class divisions. Vedic society was divided into four varnas (class divisions): the Brahmanas (priests - teaching, performing rituals), the Kshatriyas (warriors and rulers - protection and administration), the Vaishyas (farmers, traders and producers - economic support), and the Shudras (service to the other three). In the Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta the four spring from the body of the primeval being. In the Early period the division was flexible and based largely on function; by the Later Vedic period it hardened into a hereditary caste-like order, with the Brahmans claiming supremacy and the Shudras denied Vedic study.

The four Ashramas and the education system. Life was idealised in four stages (Ashramas): Brahmacharya (student life - celibate study of the Vedas under a guru), Grihastha (householder - marriage, earning, raising a family, performing sacrifices), Vanaprastha (partial retirement - forest life, contemplation) and Sannyasa (complete renunciation - seeking moksha). Education was given in the guru's home (gurukula): after the Upanayana initiation, the pupil lived with the teacher, served him, and learned the Vedas, grammar, arithmetic, ethics and skills, free of fees, ending with the samavartana (return home). Famous Later Vedic centres included Takshashila and the forest academies (e.g. of Janaka's court debates); women's education, common early, narrowed in the Later period.

blocks.text: Sabha vs Samiti: Smaller council of elders/nobles advising and judging versus the larger popular assembly that elected and could censure the king.
Early Vedic economy vs Later Vedic economy: Pastoral, cattle-wealth, barter versus agrarian, iron plough, specialised crafts, coins and regular revenue.
Early Vedic women vs Later Vedic women: Educated, visible in assemblies and ritual versus restricted to the home, early marriage and veiling.
Varna (Early) vs Varna (Later): Flexible functional division versus hereditary, rigid caste order with Brahmanical supremacy.

questions.prompt: Which is the oldest of the four Vedas?
questions.explanation: The Rig Veda, with 1,028 hymns, is the oldest Veda.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the Atharva Veda because of its folk content.

questions.prompt: The Rig Vedic popular assembly which elected the king was the:
questions.explanation: The Samiti was the broad people's assembly; the Sabha was the council of elders.

questions.prompt: Which change marks the Later Vedic economy most clearly?
options: Iron plough agriculture with permanent villages
questions.answer: Iron plough agriculture with permanent villages
questions.explanation: Iron technology made forest-clearing and deep ploughing possible, making agriculture the mainstay.

questions.prompt: Name the two great epics of the Vedic tradition.
questions.explanation: Later compiled, but rooted in the Vedic world and its values.

questions.answer: The teacher's household where a pupil lived and studied after the Upanayana ceremony.
questions.explanation: Education was residential and free, ending with samavartana.
questions.commonMistake: Describing it as a royal school for princes only.

questions.prompt: Mention any two functions of the Sabha in the Rig Vedic age.
questions.answer: Any two of: advising the king on affairs of state; performing judicial functions (hearing disputes); representing the nobles and elders of the tribe; later, sitting as the king's court.
questions.explanation: The Sabha was the king's council of elders.
questions.commonMistake: Assigning the Samiti's electoral role to the Sabha.

questions.answer: Brahmacharya (student life of celibate study), Grihastha (householder - marriage, work, family and sacrifice), Vanaprastha (partial retirement to the forest for contemplation) and Sannyasa (complete renunciation seeking liberation).
questions.explanation: Four stages of life, each with its duties.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing Ashramas with the four varnas.

questions.prompt: State the position of the king in the Early Vedic age.
questions.answer: He was a tribal leader (rajan) chosen or accepted by the people to protect the tribe and cattle and to lead in war; he was advised by the Sabha and Samiti, assisted by household officers (ratnins), received voluntary tribute (bali) rather than regular tax, and could be criticised by the assemblies - his rule was limited, not absolute.
questions.explanation: Consent, counsel and limited power are the keys.
questions.commonMistake: Describing him as an absolute monarch.

questions.prompt: Compare the position of women in Early and Later Vedic society.
questions.answer: Early Vedic women enjoyed respect and freedom: they could be educated and even compose hymns (Lopamudra, Ghosha, Apala); they attended assemblies and sacrifices, chose husbands in some cases, were not veiled, and widow remarriage seems permissible. In the Later Vedic period their position declined: education was largely denied, early marriage spread, the ideal of dependence on father-husband-son was preached, veiling appeared among some classes, and women lost their place in public life. The change followed settled agriculture, rigid varna order and ritual growth.
questions.explanation: Cover education, public role and marriage on both sides.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming women's status improved in the Later period.

questions.prompt: Compare the economy of the Early and Later Vedic periods.
questions.answer: The Early Vedic economy was pastoral and semi-nomadic: cattle were the chief wealth (war was 'gavishthi', the search for cows); land belonged to the tribe; agriculture was secondary; exchange was by barter with cows as a value-unit and nishka as high-value ornament-money; crafts were few. In the Later Vedic period, the iron ploughshare and irrigation made agriculture the mainstay with permanent villages; crafts (weaving, metal-work, Painted Grey Ware pottery) and trade specialised; coins (nishka, satamana) and regular land revenue (bali) appeared; land became individually owned. In short: pastoral tribal wealth gave way to agrarian kingdom economy.
questions.explanation: Occupation, wealth-unit, craft and revenue on both sides.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting iron's role in the transition.

questions.prompt: Describe the four-fold class divisions of Vedic society and explain how they changed from the Early to the Later Vedic period.
questions.answer: Vedic society was divided into four varnas: the Brahmanas (priests and teachers, performing rituals and preserving learning), the Kshatriyas (warriors and rulers, protecting and governing), the Vaishyas (farmers, traders and producers, supporting society economically) and the Shudras (serving the other three orders). The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta describes them as springing from the mouth, arms, thighs and feet of the primeval being. In the Early Vedic age the division was flexible and largely functional - a man's class matched his work, and movement was possible. By the Later Vedic period the system hardened into a hereditary, birth-based hierarchy: the Brahmans claimed the highest place through ritual monopoly, inter-dining and marriage were restricted, and the Shudras were denied Vedic study and dignity. Thus a functional division became a rigid caste-like order, shaping Indian society for centuries.
questions.explanation: Name all four, their duties, then the flexibile-to-rigid change.

questions.prompt: Give reasons: the Samiti is considered more 'democratic' than the Sabha.
questions.answer: The Samiti was the broad assembly of the people (visah), which elected the king, discussed public affairs and could express disapproval of a ruler - it embodied popular consent. The Sabha was a smaller body of elders and nobles acting as the king's council and court, so its membership was restricted. Wider participation and the power to make and unmake leaders give the Samiti its more democratic character.
questions.explanation: Basis of membership + powers = the reason.
questions.commonMistake: Stating the difference without explaining democracy.
